Background and Objectives: Normative modeling expresses an individual's brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus. Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested. We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy. Methods: We retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania. Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references). White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts. Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis. Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (α=0.05).

At 80% power and uncorrected α=0.05, the study could detect AUC ≥0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, ≥0.64 for focal versus generalized, and ≥0.60 for drugresistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy (Table 2). For a single true effect within the largest correction family (18 tract features), these increased to 0.70, 0.69, and 0.64. The largest observed AUCs were 0.61 (95% CI 0.50-0.72), 0.62 (0.53-0.70), and 0.60 (0.53-0.67), respectively (Fig. 5; Supplementary Table 1).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

# table data --------------------------------------

), Text = c("Group labels were randomly permuted 5,000 times; for each permutation, a t-statistic was computed at each node comparing groups, contiguous suprathreshold nodes (p<0.05) were grouped into clusters, and the maximum cluster mass was retained to form a null distribution specific to that tract.",

"Significant findings (p<0.05) bolded.")), row.names = c(NA,

# display table -----------------------------------

text.text: Background and Objectives: Normative modeling expresses an individual's brain measures as deviations from a large healthy reference and has been advanced as a route to precision imaging biomarkers in epilepsy, where structural abnormality is distributed rather than confined to the presumed focus.
Whether this framework can inform clinical classification from clinically acquired T1-weighted and diffusion MRI is untested.
We asked whether normative deviations discriminate between (1) epilepsy and functional seizures; (2) focal and generalized epilepsy; and (3) drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy.
Methods: We retrospectively studied patients with epilepsy or functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy who underwent 3-Tesla epilepsy-protocol MRI at the University of Pennsylvania.
Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references).
text.formatted: Morphometric deviation scores (cortical thickness, subcortical volume) were derived from CentileBrain (n>37,000 healthy references).

text.text: White matter fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity profiles were referenced to harmonized Human Connectome Project cohorts.

Lobar composites, hemispheric asymmetry indices, and whole-tract means were compared with rank-sum tests; discrimination was summarized as area under the ROC curve (AUC) with bootstrap confidence intervals and Benjamini-Hochberg correction.
Whole-brain deviation burden was examined as a secondary analysis.
Minimum detectable effects were estimated by Monte Carlo simulation at 80% power (α=0.05).
Results: We included 273 patients with epilepsy (203 focal, 37 generalized, 33 unclassified; 97 drug-resistant, 176 drug-responsive) and 32 with functional seizures.

In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level normative measure distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy; AUCs did not exceed 0.62, with upper confidence limits up to 0.72.

In the secondary analysis, whole-brain morphometric deviation burden was modestly higher in epilepsy than in . functional seizures (AUC 0.66, 95% CI 0.57-0.74) but did not separate the within-epilepsy comparisons.
The study could detect AUC ≥0.65 for epilepsy versus functional seizures, ≥0.64 for focal versus generalized, and ≥0.60 for drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy.
Discussion: Univariate normative deviation summaries from clinical MRI do not currently distinguish these groups well enough to guide care.
Whole-brain deviation burden, the only summary measure that differed after correction, was detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification.
Progress may require network-targeted analysis of patient-specific deviations and multimodal integration.
The evaluation and management of patients with suspected epilepsy involves a sequence of clinical decisions, each carrying diagnostic or prognostic uncertainty.
The first is determination of whether the paroxysmal events are epileptic in origin.

Functional seizures, also known as psychogenic nonepileptic seizures or events, are common, frequently mistaken for epilepsy, and a leading cause of misdiagnosis, delayed care, and unnecessary antiseizure medication (ASM) exposure. 1, 2 The second is classification of epilepsy as focal or generalized, which differ in presumed mechanism, treatment, and surgical candidacy.

text.text: The third is identifying ASM resistance, as approximately one-third of patients are drug-resistant, defined by the International League Against Epilepsy as failure of two adequate trials of appropriately chosen and tolerated antiseizure medications to achieve sustained seizure freedom. 3, 4 While growing evidence suggests that earlier surgical treatment in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy improves seizure freedom outcomes, the clinical determination of drug resistance depends on sequential trials of ASMs and is reached at a median of 10 years after epilepsy diagnosis. [5] [6] [7] Objective biomarkers could inform any of these decisions, enabling earlier interventions and improved outcomes.

text.text: Quantitative analysis of brain MRI offers objective measures that may be relevant to each of these clinical classifications.

From T1-weighted images, cortical thickness and subcortical volumes capture morphometric change, while diffusion-weighted imaging yields measures of white matter microstructure such as fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD). 8, 9 In epilepsy, structural abnormalities have been found to be widespread, extending beyond the presumed seizure focus, including distributed cortical thinning and subcortical volume loss, and altered white matter microstructure most pronounced in the corpus callosum, cingulum, and external capsule. 10, 11 Compared to generalized epilepsy, focal epilepsy showed more extensive white matter abnormalities and partly distinct regional patterns of gray matter change, alongside differences in structural network organization. 10, 12, 13 In functional seizures, the few studies comparing patients to healthy controls reported subtle, network-level differences.

text.text: These included convergent cortical thinning in visual and sensorimotor cortex and hyperconnectivity across sensorimotor, default-mode, and attentional networks, though findings came from small, heterogeneous cohorts. 14, 15 Few studies have directly compared imaging between drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy.

text.text: In idiopathic generalized epilepsy, drug-resistant patients showed more widespread FA alterations in white matter networks. 16 Structural network analyses in temporal lobe epilepsy revealed differences in global network architecture between the two groups. 17, 18 A persistent challenge across these comparisons is the heterogeneity of epilepsy, which limits the interpretability of traditional group-level analyses.

text.text: Case-control comparisons rely on population averages and may obscure meaningful individual-level variation in brain structure, a limitation compounded in focal epilepsy by uncertainty in epileptogenic network localization, particularly in cases without invasive monitoring or surgery.

Normative modeling addresses this limitation by quantifying how much an individual deviates from a reference distribution matched by age and sex, rather than relying on group averages, yielding interpretable individual-level deviation scores. 19 This framework has recently been advanced as a route to precision MRI biomarkers in epilepsy, with potential for abnormality localization and individual-level prediction. 20 Here we ask whether normative modeling is ready to inform the clinical classifications providers rely on, using clinically acquired MRI, which at our tertiary epilepsy center includes 1-mm T1-weighted and 30-direction diffusion-weighted imaging.

text.text: We applied normative models of cortical thickness, subcortical volume, and along-tract white matter microstructure to the scans from a consecutive tertiary-center cohort, and tested whether individual-level deviations can discriminate between epilepsy and functional seizures, between focal and generalized epilepsy, and between drug-resistant and drug-responsive epilepsy.
Rather than asking whether group differences exist, we asked whether individuallevel deviations discriminate these groups strongly enough to be clinically useful.
We also estimated the effect sizes this cohort could detect and the range of effects compatible with the data, so that negative findings could be interpreted as bounds.
This retrospective study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the University of Pennsylvania (protocol 835008) with a waiver of informed consent.

Normative reference data were obtained from the Human Connectome Project Young Adult and Aging datasets under their respective data use agreements; participants in those studies provided written informed consent at the originating institutions.

Epilepsy-protocol 3-Tesla MRI brain scans with both T1-weighted and 30-direction diffusion-weighted sequences were obtained from patients who were seen at the Penn Epilepsy Center at the University of Pennsylvania from May 2022 to January 2025.
Medical records were reviewed by a board-certified epileptologist (D.Z.) to determine each patient's clinical diagnosis and classification, based on the assessments of their treating epileptologists.
Patients with epilepsy and patients with functional seizures without comorbid epilepsy were included.

Patients without a clear diagnosis of either, including those with functional seizures occurring alongside epilepsy, single unprovoked or acute symptomatic seizures, or events that were not clearly epileptic, were excluded.
Among patients with epilepsy, those with prior brain surgery before the time of MRI, or without usable diffusion or morphometric data, were excluded.
Epilepsy was classified as focal, generalized, or unclassified according to the treating epileptologist's diagnosis.

Among patients treated with ASM for at least one year, drug resistance was defined according to the International League Against Epilepsy as failure of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used ASM schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom, 4 assessed at the most recent follow-up.
text.formatted: Among patients treated with ASM for at least one year, drug resistance was defined according to the International League Against Epilepsy as failure of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used ASM schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom, <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> assessed at the most recent follow-up.

text.text: Patients were classified as drug-responsive if they had been seizure-free on ASM for at least 12 consecutive months, with seizure freedom continuing through the most recent follow-up.
Patients whose treatment response could not be clearly determined, such as those with continued seizures after only a single medication trial, were excluded from the study (Supplementary Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Patients whose treatment response could not be clearly determined, such as those with continued seizures after only a single medication trial, were excluded from the study (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Extracted clinical metadata included age at first seizure, epilepsy duration, history of convulsive seizures or status epilepticus, presence of an epileptogenic lesion on MRI, and presence of interictal epileptiform discharges on routine or ambulatory EEG.
Epilepsy duration was calculated from the date of first seizure to the date of the MRI scan.
Presence of an epileptogenic lesion was determined by the treating epileptologist.
MRI scans of the clinical cohort were acquired at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania on Siemens 3T scanners.
T1-weighted images were acquired using a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo (MPRAGE) sequence at 1.0 mm isotropic resolution.

Diffusion-weighted images were acquired with a single-shell echo-planar imaging sequence comprising 30 diffusion-encoding directions at b = 1000 s/mm² and one nondiffusion-weighted (b = 0) volume, at a native resolution of 2.2 mm isotropic.

A separate b = 0 volume with reversed phase-encoding direction was acquired to estimate the susceptibility-induced B0 field, and the resulting geometric distortions were corrected during preprocessing using FSL topup. 21 Cortical thickness and subcortical volumes were estimated from T1-weighted images using FreeSurfer (version 7.3.2) 22 with the Desikan-Killiany atlas, 23 yielding 68 cortical and 14 subcortical regions of interest.

text.text: White matter tract profiles were reconstructed using pyAFQ (version 2.1), 25 yielding FA and MD, sampled at 100 nodes along each of 16 bundles.
text.formatted: White matter tract profiles were reconstructed using pyAFQ (version 2.1), <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> yielding FA and MD, sampled at 100 nodes along each of 16 bundles.

text.text: The middle cerebellar peduncle was excluded, as brainstem tractography is prone to susceptibility-induced distortion and artifactual contamination by crossing fibers. 26

text.text: Deviation scores were derived separately for morphometry and tractometry, each expressing an individual's brain measures as a deviation from an age-and sex-matched healthy reference population (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Deviation scores were derived separately for morphometry and tractometry, each expressing an individual's brain measures as a deviation from an age-and sex-matched healthy reference population (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: For morphometry, z-scores for cortical thickness and subcortical volume were obtained from CentileBrain, which used pretrained sex-specific models expressing each region as a standardized residual adjusting for age, sex, intracranial volume for subcortical volumes, and mean cortical thickness for cortical thickness. 27 These models were derived from over 37,000 healthy individuals aged 3-90.

text.text: Cortical thickness and subcortical volumes were extracted with FreeSurfer 7.3.2, and the corresponding scanner vendor (Siemens) and FreeSurfer version were provided to CentileBrain as covariates.

For tractometry, z-scores for FA and MD along tracts were referenced to healthy subjects from the Human Connectome Project (HCP) Young Adult (ages 22-35, 1064 subjects) and Aging (ages 36-100+, 1365 subjects) datasets, 28, 29 preprocessed with the HCP minimal preprocessing pipelines. 30 Diffusion tensors were fit to the b = 1000 s/mm² shell for HCP Young Adult and to the b = 1500 s/mm² shell for HCP Aging, which has no b = 1000 shell.

text.text: Missing left-fornix profiles (22 clinical and 46 HCP scans) were replaced with the pooled mean.

Site-and protocol-related variance was removed with neuroCombat (version 0.2.12), 31 with acquisition site as the batch variable (six sites: HCP Young Adult, the four HCP Aging sites, and Penn), age and sex as protected covariates, and site parameters estimated from all scans without a reference batch.

text.text: As deviations shared by all patients may be partly absorbed into site effects and harmonization can distort the normative age curve, we repeated all tractometry comparisons without harmonization and with site parameters estimated from reference subjects only (Supplementary Fig. 4).

text.text: Following harmonization, each tract and metric was regressed on age and sex in the reference subjects only (the HCP cohorts and 26 syncope patients who underwent the same epilepsy-protocol imaging), and each patient's value was expressed as a standardized residual.
Deviations for the 42 patients (14%) younger than 22 years of age (39 with epilepsy, 3 with functional seizures) relied on extrapolation below the HCP age range.
The syncope reference patients had a median age of 33.4 years (IQR 26.0-48.6), versus 36.0 years (IQR 26.0-46.0) in the analyzed cohort.
Region-level measures were aggregated for statistical analyses.

For morphometry, ROI z-scores were averaged (unweighted) within seven regional groups (frontal, temporal, parietal, occipital, insula, thalamus, and basal ganglia), combining cortical and subcortical structures where both contributed (hippocampus and amygdala within the temporal group; caudate, putamen, pallidum, and nucleus accumbens as basal ganglia; thalamus alone).
Composite z-scores retained their sign, so that negative values indicate lower thickness or volume than expected.

A lobe-level asymmetry index was computed as the absolute difference between left and right hemisphere mean z-scores, without normalization by the bilateral sum, which is unstable when z-scores approach zero.

For tractometry, left and right homologues of each paired tract were averaged node-by-node, and commissural tracts were used as reconstructed, yielding nine tract profiles (six paired bilateral tracts and three commissural tracts) of 100 nodes each.
For each profile, a tract-level mean z-score summarized overall deviation, while the full node-wise profile was retained for along-tract analysis.

Analyses were performed in Python using scipy and statsmodels. 32, 33 Group demographics were compared using Fisher's exact test for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tests for continuous variables.

text.text: Three imaging comparisons were performed: epilepsy versus functional seizures, focal versus generalized epilepsy, and drug-resistant versus drug-responsive epilepsy.
Because normative z-scores were derived from age-and sex-stratified reference models, no additional covariate adjustment was applied in the primary analyses.
Imaging features were analyzed at two scales: region/tract-level summary scores and node-wise along-tract profiles.
Lobar composite z-scores, hemispheric asymmetry indices (|z left -z right |), and tract-level mean z-scores (FA and MD) were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests.

Discriminability was quantified as the area under the curve (AUC = P(group_a > group_b)), reported as max(AUC, 1 -AUC) with the direction of each effect given separately, with 95% confidence intervals from 5,000 bootstrap resamples.
text.formatted: Discriminability was quantified as the area under the curve (AUC = P(group_a > group_b)), reported as max(AUC, 1 -AUC) with the direction of each effect given separately, with 95% confidence intervals from 5,000 bootstrap resamples.

text.text: Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied within each feature family per comparison (lobar composite z-scores, asymmetry indices, and pooled FA+MD tract z-scores).
Two secondary analyses were performed.

First, whole-brain deviation burden was summarized per patient as the number of regions with |z|>2 and the mean |z| across the 82 morphometric regions, the 18 tract-level FA and MD z-scores, and the 3,000 node-level z-scores of the 15 bundles without left-right averaging, with correction across these six measures; the epilepsy versus functional seizures comparison was repeated in non-lesional epilepsy.
text.formatted: First, whole-brain deviation burden was summarized per patient as the number of regions with |z|>2 and the mean |z| across the 82 morphometric regions, the 18 tract-level FA and MD z-scores, and the 3,000 node-level z-scores of the 15 bundles without left-right averaging, with correction across these six measures; the epilepsy versus functional seizures comparison was repeated in non-lesional epilepsy.

text.text: Second, the mean hippocampal zscore and hippocampal asymmetry index were compared, with correction across the two measures.

As a positive control, these measures were compared between patients with unilateral mesial temporal sclerosis and no other lesion and patients with non-lesional epilepsy, and the sclerotic hippocampus was compared with the contralateral side (Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
Along-tract differences in FA and MD were assessed using cluster-based permutation testing, without covariate adjustment.

Group labels were randomly permuted 5,000 times; for each permutation, a t-statistic was computed at each node comparing groups, contiguous suprathreshold nodes (p<0.05) were grouped into clusters, and the maximum cluster mass was retained to form a null distribution specific to that tract.
text.formatted: Group labels were randomly permuted 5,000 times; for each permutation, a t-statistic was computed at each node comparing groups, contiguous suprathreshold nodes (p<0.05) were grouped into clusters, and the maximum cluster mass was retained to form a null distribution specific to that tract.

text.text: Observed clusters were tested against this tract-specific null, controlling the family-wise error rate across nodes within each tract.
As all bilateral tracts were surveyed, along-tract findings were considered exploratory.

Minimum detectable effect sizes were estimated for each comparison by Monte Carlo simulation (3,000 iterations per candidate effect size), assuming normally distributed scores with equal variance and a location shift between groups, using each comparison's achieved sample sizes, 80% power, and a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test at α=0.05, both uncorrected and at α=0.05/18 (a single true effect within the largest feature family after correction).
Effects were expressed as the minimum detectable AUC.

text.text: Normative modeling of clinical epilepsy-protocol MRI did not reliably discriminate between the clinical groups we tested.

In the primary analyses, no regional or tract-level measure (lobar composite, hemispheric asymmetry, or whole-tract mean) distinguished epilepsy from functional seizures, focal from generalized epilepsy, or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy.

In secondary analyses, neither hippocampal measure separated the groups, and the one significant difference was in whole-brain deviation burden, which was higher in epilepsy than in functional seizures (AUC 0.66) and partly reflected visible lesions (AUC 0.62 in non-lesional epilepsy), an effect detectable at the group level but insufficient for individual-level classification.
Even the largest regional or tract-level effect compatible with these data (upper confidence limit 0.72) would not be actionable.

Under a binormal model, an AUC of 0.72 corresponds to about 32% sensitivity at 90% specificity, whereas discrimination conventionally considered outstanding (AUC ≥0.90) 35 would be a reasonable minimum before such a marker could inform decisions such as withdrawing ASM.

text.text: Within the precision of this cohort, univariate normative deviation summaries did not reach a level of discrimination that could inform clinical care.
The gap between group-level effects and individual-level discrimination has also been reported for normative modeling in other disorders.

In schizophrenia, normative modeling of harmonized diffusion MRI in 601 patients and 512 controls produced larger group-level effects in deviation scores than in raw measures, yet summary deviation measures classified individuals at AUC below 0.63; only combining tracts and diffusion measures exceeded 0.70. 36 Our findings followed the same pattern: whole-brain deviation burden and hippocampal asymmetry differed at the group level, but neither discriminated individuals well.

text.text: Structural correlates have been reported in both epilepsy and functional seizures, but they differ in extent and consistency.

In functional seizures, findings have been subtle and variable across studies, including superior temporal and occipital cortical changes and reduced motor and premotor cortical thickness and volume. 38, 39 In epilepsy, large-scale analyses have established widespread cortical thinning and subcortical volume reduction, but the abnormalities shared by all epilepsy groups are modest against healthy controls: lower right thalamic volume (Cohen's d 0.24-0.73) and lower bilateral precentral cortical thickness (d 0.34-0.52), corresponding to AUCs of roughly 0.57-0.70 and 0.60-0.64. 10 These effects lie largely at or below this cohort's minimum detectable effect, and the expected separation from functional seizures, which carry their own structural deviations, is smaller than that from healthy controls, consistent with the weak separation observed here.

text.text: The hippocampal positive control illustrates the gap between group-level and individual-level effects.

In mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis, group analyses report large reductions in ipsilateral hippocampal volume (d = 1.73-1.91, AUC ≈ 0.90). 10 Here, hippocampal asymmetry separated unilateral mesial temporal sclerosis from non-lesional epilepsy, but marked volume loss (≥3 SD) was present in only a third of patients.

text.text: Hippocampal sclerosis is diagnosed from T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and loss of internal architecture as well as atrophy, and these features can occur without measurable volume loss on T1-weighted MRI.
Even for this lesion, the large effect reported in group analyses did not translate into consistent individual-level deviation.
In the primary analyses, no summary-level measure separated the groups in either within-epilepsy comparison, and differences were confined to short along-tract segments.

These findings were exploratory, although the focal-generalized differences were directionally consistent with a meta-analysis reporting more pronounced white matter change in focal epilepsy. 12 The segments were predominantly in long association and commissural pathways, which have been shown to be affected across epilepsy syndromes. 11 Such a shared signal could produce weak group-level differences while lacking the specificity to distinguish focal from generalized or drug-resistant from drug-responsive epilepsy.

text.text: Because epileptogenic networks vary across patients, the deviation common to a clinical group is likely small, suggesting that classification may require multimodal features rather than further refinement of single-modality summary scores.
Several limitations should be considered.

This was a single-site, cross-sectional study, and clinical diagnosis, epilepsy type, and drug-response status were determined by retrospective review rather than independent adjudication or a uniform confirmatory protocol, so misclassification cannot be excluded.
Because normative z-scores were already age-and sex-referenced, no further covariate adjustment was applied, leaving within-epilepsy comparisons unadjusted for clinical differences between groups.
Epilepsy duration, for example, was longer in drug-resistant patients, possibly reflecting referral patterns, and could contribute to the diffusivity differences observed.
Without presurgical evaluation, the epileptogenic zone could not be localized, and without seizure frequency data, imaging differences could not be separated from cumulative seizure burden.
Excluding patients with prior brain surgery was necessary for methodological consistency but may have omitted the most severe cases.
The normative references introduced further limitations.

CentileBrain model fit varied across regions (Supplementary Table 2), with the weakest fit in the medial occipital cortex (explained variance 0.08-0.14 for pericalcarine), and some composites deviated from zero in every group (e.g., occipital, thalamus, and basal ganglia; Figs. 2 3 4), probably reflecting site calibration.

text.text: Future work could focus on the networks implicated in each patient's epilepsy.

Normative modeling yields patient-specific, spatially distributed deviations, but groups here were compared one region or tract at a time, so deviations confined to a patient's epileptogenic network would be diluted by unaffected regions and by other patients' differently located deviations.
Localization from semiology, EEG, or presurgical evaluation could restrict analyses to the presumed epileptogenic network and align deviations to the focus.
Alternatively, clustering deviation patterns across patients could identify subtypes and the modalities best suited to stratify them.

Finer spatial sampling may also help, as cortical deviations here were averaged within large parcels and lobes, and the reconstructed bundles omitted superficial white matter, where abnormalities in temporal lobe epilepsy are prominent. 42, 43 Finally, the diffusion tensor assumes Gaussian diffusion and cannot capture the non-Gaussian diffusion arising from tissue microstructure; in temporal lobe epilepsy, non-Gaussian measures, which require multi-shell acquisitions, showed greater abnormality than conventional diffusivity in association white matter. 44 In a consecutive cohort imaged on a clinical epilepsy protocol, normative modeling of structural and diffusion MRI could not classify epilepsy by type or treatment response and separated epilepsy from functional seizures only weakly, through whole-brain deviation burden.

text.text: Upper confidence limits remained below the discrimination required for clinical use, indicating that any individual-level signal in univariate deviation summaries is too small to be clinically informative.

Normative modeling remains a powerful framework for characterizing distributed abnormalities in epilepsy, but regional deviation scores from clinical MRI are not yet ready to guide these classifications, and network-targeted, multimodal approaches may be needed to achieve clinically useful discrimination.
